content.overview: Shelf-life or storage-period claims should be tied to defined product, package, conditions, methods and timepoints. A single passing result is not a stability trend.

vocabulary.definition: Scheduled sampling event in a stability plan.
Controlled sample kept for future examination under defined conditions.
Evaluation of comparable results across time to detect direction, rate or atypical change.

sections.title: Define the claim before collecting data
sections.body: The plan should state product, package, conditions, attributes, methods and decision roles. Data from another configuration may be contextual but not equivalent.

sections.title: Preserve comparable measurement context
sections.body: Sample identity, handling, method and units must remain consistent or differences must be explained. Laboratory competence and measurement comparability matter.

sections.title: Investigate atypical trends without rewriting history
sections.body: Unexpected results should retain original data and trigger controlled review rather than deletion, substitution or selective reporting.

workedExamples: A later result changes after a method revision; the trend review documents the method change instead of treating all values as directly equivalent.
commonMistakes: Calling one timepoint a shelf-life study.
Changing storage conditions without recording it.
Dropping inconvenient results from a graph.
content.practicalApplication: Draft a stability matrix linking lots, package configurations, conditions, timepoints, methods, attributes and exception handling.
content.summary: Defensible stability claims depend on predefined, comparable and traceable evidence over time.
